> **Educational summary — not medical advice.** This note is reference material for a software

## Call emergency services immediately

Any sudden onset of the following is treated as a stroke until proven otherwise:

- **Face** — drooping on one side, or an uneven smile.
- **Arm** — weakness or numbness in one arm, or one arm drifting downward when both are raised.
- **Speech** — slurred speech, difficulty finding words, or difficulty understanding others.
- **Time** — note the time symptoms began, or the last time the person was known to be well, and
  call emergency services now.

Symptoms beyond the four above that carry the same urgency: sudden numbness or weakness of the leg
or of one whole side; sudden confusion; sudden loss or blurring of vision in one or both eyes;
sudden difficulty walking, dizziness, or loss of balance and coordination; and sudden severe
headache with no known cause.

## Why the time of onset matters so much

Treatments that restore blood flow to the brain — clot-dissolving drugs and mechanical clot removal
— are effective only within a limited window from symptom onset, and their benefit falls steeply
with every passing minute. The single most useful piece of information a caller can provide is when
the person was last known to be well. Where symptoms were present on waking, the relevant time is
when the person was last seen normal, not when they woke.

Brain tissue is lost continuously while an artery is blocked. This is the reason emergency services
are called rather than waiting for a routine appointment or driving to a clinic, and the reason a
stroke is treated as time-critical in the same way as a heart attack.

## Symptoms that resolve are still an emergency

Symptoms that disappear within minutes may indicate a transient ischemic attack. The event itself
has ended, but the risk of a full stroke in the following days is substantially raised, and it is
highest in the first 48 hours. Resolution is not reassurance and does not convert this into a
routine appointment — urgent assessment is what reduces the subsequent risk.

## What not to do

Do not give food, drink, or medication, including aspirin, to someone with suspected stroke:
swallowing may be impaired, and the type of stroke — clot or bleed — determines the treatment and
cannot be established without imaging. Do not wait to see whether symptoms improve. Do not let the
person drive.

## While waiting

Keep the person resting, comfortable and observed, note the time of onset and what was observed, and
gather a list of their medications if it can be done without leaving them unattended. Anticoagulant
use is particularly important for the receiving team to know.

This system does not diagnose. Any presentation matching this note is escalated, and no answer it

## Call emergency services immediately

Any sudden onset of the following is treated as a stroke until proven otherwise:

- **Face** — drooping on one side, or an uneven smile.
- **Arm** — weakness or numbness in one arm, or one arm drifting downward when both are raised.
- **Speech** — slurred speech, difficulty finding words, or difficulty understanding others.
- **Time** — note the time symptoms began, or the last time the person was known to be well, and
  call emergency services now.

Symptoms beyond the four above that carry the same urgency: sudden numbness or weakness of the leg
or of one whole side; sudden confusion; sudden loss or blurring of vision in one or both eyes;
sudden difficulty walking, dizziness, or loss of balance and coordination; and sudden severe
headache with no known cause.

## Why the time of onset matters so much

Treatments that restore blood flow to the brain — clot-dissolving drugs and mechanical clot removal
— are effective only within a limited window from symptom onset, and their benefit falls steeply
with every passing minute. The single most useful piece of information a caller can provide is when
the person was last known to be well. Where symptoms were present on waking, the relevant time is
when the person was last seen normal, not when they woke.

Brain tissue is lost continuously while an artery is blocked. This is the reason emergency services
are called rather than waiting for a routine appointment or driving to a clinic, and the reason a
stroke is treated as time-critical in the same way as a heart attack.

## Symptoms that resolve are still an emergency

Symptoms that disappear within minutes may indicate a transient ischemic attack. The event itself
has ended, but the risk of a full stroke in the following days is substantially raised, and it is
highest in the first 48 hours. Resolution is not reassurance and does not convert this into a
routine appointment — urgent assessment is what reduces the subsequent risk.

## What not to do

Do not give food, drink, or medication, including aspirin, to someone with suspected stroke:
swallowing may be impaired, and the type of stroke — clot or bleed — determines the treatment and
cannot be established without imaging. Do not wait to see whether symptoms improve. Do not let the
person drive.

## While waiting

Keep the person resting, comfortable and observed, note the time of onset and what was observed, and
gather a list of their medications if it can be done without leaving them unattended. Anticoagulant
use is particularly important for the receiving team to know.

This system does not diagnose. Any presentation matching this note is escalated, and no answer it
produces is a substitute for emergency assessment.

`supported`. So is a claim that **aggregates or generalizes** several source statements into one
sentence, as long as every part it asserts appears somewhere in the sources — cite the source
carrying the main part. Requiring the answer to echo the source is grading style, not grounding.

**A rationale the sources do not give is a separate claim.** Where the sources state a rule and the
answer explains *why* the rule exists — in terms of billing, reimbursement, record complexity, or
any motivation the sources are silent on — the rule is one claim and is `supported`, and the
rationale is a second claim and is `unsupported`. Do not let the supported half carry the other.

### The specific-attribute check

Run this before you write `supported`. **Topical overlap is not support**: a claim and a source can
be about the same document, the same condition and the same paragraph and still not match. Check
that the source agrees with the claim on each of:

- the **object** the fact attaches to — which measure, which drug class, which body system, which
  test;
- the **threshold or number** — the value, the unit, and the direction of the comparison;
- the **mechanism or cause** it names;
- the **population or condition** it applies to.

A claim that takes a fact the sources state about one object, threshold, mechanism or population
and attaches it to a **different** one is `contradicted`, not `supported`. Worked example: the
sources describe an action plan built on daily weight change and fluid-retention warning signs, and
the answer says patients are given an action plan for salt intake. Same note, same condition, wrong
object — that is `contradicted`.

### Claims about the sources themselves

A sentence asserting what the SOURCES do or do not contain — "the passage does not list the
specific classes", "the retrieved material does not name a threshold" — **is a claim**, and it is
checked against the sources rather than waved through. Read the sources and decide. If a source
does contain what the answer says is absent, the claim is `contradicted`.

### Evidence for every verdict that is not `unsupported`

Every claim you mark `supported` must carry **the number of the source that supports it** and a
**short verbatim span copied from that source** — at most 25 words — in `quote`. If you cannot copy
a span that carries the claim, the verdict is not `supported`.

A `contradicted` claim carries the number of the source it contradicts and the span that
contradicts it. An `unsupported` claim carries `"source": null` and an empty `quote`.
